summary: Year 5 'Earth and space': build the heliocentric model — the Sun (a star) at the centre with Earth and the other planets orbiting it, the Moon orbiting Earth while Earth orbits the Sun, and the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies. The core difficulty is the deep geocentric intuition and the nested two-orbit system (Moon to Earth, Earth to Sun), plus a flat-disc reading of the bodies. Teach it with enacted/physical models children move themselves, a top-down orbit model they run and compare against observation, explicit sphericity evidence, and the history of ideas (Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, Alhazen's critique of it, and Copernicus's Sun-centred model).
misconceptions: The Sun orbits or goes around the Earth (the geocentric model), or everything orbits Earth.
The Sun, Earth and Moon are flat discs rather than spheres.
The Moon orbits the Sun directly, rather than orbiting Earth while both orbit the Sun.
The Sun is somehow different from 'a star'.
Planets are close together and similar in size (a scale error from diagrams); Pluto is still a planet.

activities.title: Be the Earth, the Moon and the Sun — enact the nested orbits
steps: In a group of three, place a lamp or ball as the Sun. One child is the Earth and walks a slow circle around the Sun.
The 'Moon' child circles the 'Earth' child continuously WHILE the Earth keeps walking its orbit around the Sun, so both motions happen at once.
Pause and say aloud: 'The Moon goes around the Earth, and the Earth (with the Moon) goes around the Sun.'
Swap roles so every child has been the Moon that must keep looping its Earth while the Earth travels.
activities.insight: The Moon orbits Earth while the Earth–Moon pair together travel round the Sun — two simultaneous, nested orbits, not the Moon circling the Sun directly.

activities.title: Run and compare a top-down solar-system model
steps: Run a top-down view: the planets glide around the Sun while the Moon circles the Earth. Use a time slider to speed up, slow down or scrub the motion.
Watch specifically for the Moon looping the Earth AT THE SAME TIME as the Earth loops the Sun, and describe this nesting in your own words.
Flip a toggle to an Earth-centred arrangement (Sun and everything circling the Earth) and compare it with the Sun-centred one.

Compare the two using concrete things the model shows: notice that the Moon circles the Earth in both arrangements, so look at the planets. In which arrangement do the planets' paths, including times when a planet seems to drift backwards across our sky, come out more simply? Explain your choice.
activities.insight: The Sun-centred model, with the Moon still orbiting Earth, accounts for the planets' observed motions more simply; together with later observations, this is why it replaced the earlier Earth-centred model.

activities.title: Spheres, not discs — gather the evidence
steps: Handle a globe lit by a single light source and describe how light falls on a ball versus a flat disc.
Look at real photographs of the Sun, Earth and Moon taken from space and state whether each is a ball or a flat circle.

List evidence that the bodies are spheres: photos from space of all three; for Earth, the curved shadow it casts on the Moon during a lunar eclipse and ships disappearing hull-first over the horizon; for the Moon, the curved edge between its lit and dark parts as its phases change.
Say the conclusion in full: 'The Sun, Earth and Moon are approximately spherical.'
activities.insight: The Sun, Earth and Moon are approximately spherical bodies, not flat discs drawn on a flat sky.

activities.title: Name and order the planets; test what-orbits-what
steps: Name the planets in order out from the Sun and state that they all orbit the Sun.
Match each body to what it orbits: Moon to Earth; Earth and the other planets to the Sun.
Answer a geocentric-vs-heliocentric choice: which arrangement has the Sun at the centre, and why is it the accepted one?
Sort pictures or statements into 'sphere' versus 'flat disc' for the Sun, Earth and Moon.
activities.insight: Consolidate the model: Sun at the centre as a star, planets orbiting it in order, the Moon orbiting Earth, all three bodies spherical.

activities.title: Interview Copernicus — why move the Sun to the centre? (optional history companion)
steps: In role, or questioning a peer in role as Copernicus, ask: 'Why isn't the Earth at the centre?'
Draw out that placing the Sun at the centre accounted for the observed motions more simply than the earlier Earth-centred model.

Connect the story to the model: Ptolemy set out a detailed Earth-centred model, Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham) criticised problems in Ptolemy's model, and Copernicus proposed putting the Sun at the centre; later observations by others helped it become accepted.
activities.insight: The counter-intuitive heliocentric model became accepted because it accounted for observations more simply and was supported by later observations (such as Galileo's telescope discoveries) — the history makes the model credible.

checkQuestion: Tell me the path of the Moon: what does the Moon go around, and what does THAT thing go around? … Now, how do you know the Earth travels round the Sun and not the other way?
checkAnswer: The Moon orbits the Earth; the Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun — so the Moon circles the Earth while the pair together travel round the Sun, which sits at the centre. The Earth is a planet like the others, and the Sun is a star.
